label: Colossians 1:3–8
text:
Paul's word for "praying" is proseuchomai, built on the preposition pros, "toward" — it pictures prayer offered face-to-face with God, never used elsewhere in the New Testament for requests made to a person. The Colossians' faith rests "in" Christ (a preposition of settled position, not motion into), while their love reaches "into" the other saints — the difference is a faith already at home versus a love still pressing forward to embrace others. That love and faith are fueled by a hope "laid up" for them in heaven: the verb is a perfect participle of a word meaning "to be stored away," picturing something deposited once and kept safe ever since, beyond the reach of any thief or enemy. The gospel itself, Paul says, is "bearing fruit and increasing" — both verbs are middle voice, marking an energy that comes from within the plant itself rather than being applied from outside, like a seed carrying its own capacity to reproduce.

Paul's petition for the church turns to a specific word for knowledge, epignosis — gnosis with the prefix epi- added, intensifying it into a full, penetrating grasp rather than a surface acquaintance. It was a favorite term of the very teachers troubling Colossae, who reserved "true knowledge" for an inner circle; Paul prays that all the saints be filled with it, refusing to let it stay exclusive. Their conduct is to be "worthy" of the Lord — axios, literally "of equal weight," conduct that tips the scale to match the character of the One they represent.

Being "strengthened with might" pairs a verb and noun from the same root (dynamoo / dynamis) — strength that gives actual capacity to act, not just theoretical power — measured "according to" the manifested strength of God's glory. Two different words render as "patience": makrothymia is patience worn toward difficult people, staying power that refuses to blaze up in anger at provocation; hypomone is endurance under circumstances, the grit that holds up under a long siege of trouble. "Made us meet" translates hikanoo, "to render sufficient" — it describes God qualifying believers for their share in the saints' inheritance by placing them, once for all, in a standing that already qualifies them.
translation: I am continually giving thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying for you, since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and the love you continually hold toward all the saints, on account of the hope stored away for you in heaven — the hope you heard of before in the message of the gospel's truth, which has arrived and is at home among you, just as it is in all the world, continually bearing its own fruit and increasing, just as it has been doing among you from the day you heard and came to know experientially the grace of God in truth. We have not stopped praying for you and asking that you be filled with the full, penetrating knowledge of His will in every wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk in a manner weighing as much as the Lord, pleasing Him in everything, continually bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the full knowledge of God, being made powerful with all power according to the strength of His glory, resulting in all endurance and patience-toward-people with joy, giving thanks to the Father who qualified you for a share of the portion of the saints in light.

label: Colossians 1:13
text: The verb "delivered" is rhyomai, which pictures rescue by force — being drawn out and away by someone stronger, not a quiet transfer. What we're delivered from is "the power of darkness," exousia — not lawful, ordered authority but its opposite, an arbitrary, tyrannical grip; darkness rules by domination, not by right. What we're delivered into is a basileia, a properly ordered kingdom under a rightful king, the sharpest possible contrast to the rule just left behind. "Translated" renders methistemi, the word used for the wholesale relocation of conquered peoples by ancient empires — moving an entire population from one territory and reseating it in another. Paul pictures the believer's transfer out of Satan's domain into Christ's kingdom on that scale: not a change of mood but a change of citizenship.
translation: Who rescued us out of the tyrannical dominion of the darkness and resettled us into the kingdom of the Son of His love.

label: Colossians 1:14
text: "Redemption" translates apolytrosis, a term for release purchased by paying a ransom price — not a favor extended but a debt settled. Paul immediately defines that redemption as "forgiveness," aphesis, literally a "sending away" — the same idea pictured in the Day of Atonement scapegoat, which carried Israel's sins out of the camp and out of sight for good. At the cross, sin isn't overlooked; it's paid for and then sent away.
translation: In whom we continually hold our release, secured by the payment of a ransom — the sending away of our sins.

label: Colossians 1:15
text: "Image" translates eikon, a word that implies derivation from an original — not an accidental resemblance, the way two eggs happen to look alike, but a copy struck from a die, the way a coin bears the sovereign's likeness or a child bears the parent's features. Applied to Christ, it means He is God's exact, derived representation. "Firstborn," prototokos, carries two ideas at once in Greek usage: priority in time and primacy in rank. It doesn't put Christ inside the class of created things as the first specimen; it places Him before all creation and over it — the eternal Son, not the first thing made.
translation: Who is the derived likeness of the unseen God, having priority over and sovereignty over all creation.

label: Colossians 1:16
text: "The all things" — ta panta with the article, meaning the entire, collective universe rather than a scattered list of items — "were created," first in the aorist tense, marking one definite, completed act at a point in the past. The preposition rendered "by Him" is actually locative, "in Him": creation didn't merely pass through Christ as a tool, it took place within the sphere of His person, as though His very being were the space in which the universe came to exist. A second appearance of "created" near the end of the verse shifts to the perfect tense — the act is past, but the result stands permanently: everything remains, right now, in a state of having-been-created by Him. Everything moves toward Him too, not just from Him — the same things that owe their origin to Christ also owe Him their destiny.
translation: Because in Him were created the all things — the ones in the heavens and the ones on the earth, the visible things and the invisible — whether thrones or lordships or rulers or authorities; the all things stand created through Him and with a view to Him.

label: Colossians 1:17
text: "He Himself is before all things" — the pronoun autos is thrown in for emphasis where Greek doesn't require it, underlining His personal identity, while the verb "is" (not "was" or "became") states plain, timeless existence prior to everything that had a beginning. "Consist" is synistemi in the perfect tense — literally "hold together" — picturing Christ as the ongoing principle of cohesion that keeps the universe an ordered system rather than a chaos of disconnected parts. Whatever holds atoms together or keeps galaxies in their courses, Paul says, is an expression of His sustaining will, continuously exercised, not a force set going once and left alone.
translation: And He Himself is before all things, and the all things continue holding together in Him.

label: Colossians 1:18
text: "Beginning," arche, again doubles as both "point of origin" and "governing source" — Christ isn't merely first in a sequence of church history, He's the one from whom the church's life originates. "Firstborn from the dead" pictures resurrection as a kind of birth, Christ emerging from among the dead the way an infant emerges from the womb — the same image lies behind the phrase elsewhere about God "loosing the birth-pangs of death." The verb behind "might have the preeminence" is a form of ginomai, "become," not the verb "to be" used of His eternal deity back in verse 15 — a careful distinction: Christ is eternally first by nature, but He became head of the church in time, through incarnation and resurrection, entering that headship as a historical event layered on top of an eternal fact.
translation: And He Himself is the Head of the body, the church; who is the origin, firstborn out from among the dead, in order that He might become — in all things — Himself the One holding first place.

label: Colossians 1:19
text: "Dwell" is katoikeo, built on the word for "home" with the prefix kata- added for emphasis — a permanent residence, not the temporary lodging pictured by a related word for sojourning as a stranger. Paul is saying that the full weight of deity doesn't visit Christ or rest on Him temporarily; it is permanently at home in Him, as native to His being as a family living in its own house rather than borrowed lodgings. "Fulness," pleroma, is a term the false teachers at Colossae liked to use for the sum-total of divine power, which they imagined as parceled out among a chain of lesser spiritual beings. Paul's point is blunt: none of it is divided or diluted — the entire pleroma, undivided, is at home in Christ alone.
translation: Because in Him God was well pleased that all the fulness continually make its permanent home.

label: Colossians 1:20
text:
"To make peace" translates a verb whose root sense is "to bind together" — Christ's death doesn't simply end hostilities, it welds back together what sin had torn apart. "Reconcile" is compounded with the preposition apo, "back" or "away from" — restoration to an original, prior unity, not the creation of something new. Paul extends the reach of that reconciliation to "things on earth" and "things in heaven," cosmic in scope, all of it secured through the blood of His cross — the single price by which both the estrangement of guilty people and the disorder of a groaning creation are addressed.

Verses 21–22 pick up the same thread for individual believers. "Alienated" is a perfect passive participle — a settled, once-established state of estrangement, not a passing mood. "Enemies" carries an active sense: hostility in mind, not just outward hostility suffered. And "present you holy" pictures a searching, penetrating gaze — the compound word for "sight" builds "look down into," the inspection of someone examining an object up close, and Paul says believers will stand that scrutiny blameless.
translation: And, through Him, to reconcile the all things to Himself, having made peace by the blood of His cross — whether the things on the earth or the things in the heavens. And you, who once were in a settled state of alienation and hostile in mind because of your evil deeds, He has now reconciled in the body of His flesh through death, in order to present you holy and without blemish and beyond reproach before His penetrating gaze.

label: Colossians 1:23
text: "Assuming" translates ei with the indicative mood — not the hypothetical "if" that leaves the outcome open, but a conditional particle used with a fact already assumed true, closer to "since" than "if perhaps." Paul isn't questioning whether the Colossians are saved; continuing in the faith is the evidence, not the condition, of a salvation already secured. "Grounded" is a perfect participle of a verb meaning "to lay a foundation" — a once-for-all act with lasting results: they were set on the foundation, and they remain set on it. Genuine faith doesn't need to be topped up by the new teachers' additions; it rests, complete, on a foundation already laid.
translation: Since, as is the case, you continue in your faith, having been placed on a foundation with the present result that you stand firmly grounded, and are not being shifted away from the hope held out by the gospel you heard — the gospel proclaimed in all creation under heaven, of which I, Paul, became a servant.

label: Colossians 1:24
text: "Fill up" is a compound verb, antanapleroo, whose prefix anti- signals that what's supplied comes from a corresponding, matching source, filling a gap from the opposite side. The "afflictions of Christ" here is not the word Paul elsewhere uses of His atoning death — that term never describes His sacrificial suffering on the cross — but the suffering He endured in His earthly ministry: opposition, persecution, exhaustion in service. That kind of suffering was necessarily cut short by His limited years on earth, and Paul pictures himself and every faithful servant since as continuing to supply what that curtailed ministry left unfinished, in the ongoing work of building up the church, His body.
translation: I am now rejoicing in my sufferings on your behalf, and on my part filling up what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ, in my flesh, for the sake of His body, which is the church.

label: Colossians 1:25
text: "Dispensation" is oikonomia, built from "house" and "law" — the term for a household steward's job of administering the master's affairs, not owning them but managing them faithfully on someone else's behalf. Paul describes his apostleship the same way: a stewardship entrusted to him, not a possession he earned. "Fulfil the word of God" doesn't mean merely finishing a task but giving the message its complete development — preaching it out to its full intended scope, Gentile and Jew alike, so nothing of its content is left undelivered.
translation: Of which I became a servant, according to the stewardship of God given to me for you, to give full development to the word of God.

label: Colossians 1:26
text: "Mystery" borrows a word familiar from the pagan mystery religions, but Paul turns its meaning inside out. Where those cults guarded their secrets for a narrow circle of initiates, the Christian "mystery" is a truth once hidden that is now announced to everyone — the very opposite of exclusivity. It was hidden "from" the ages, not "before" them: concealment could only begin once there were people from whom to conceal it, so the hiding starts with humanity's history, even though God's purpose was fixed before the world began.
translation: The mystery that has been kept hidden from the ages and from the generations, but has now been made known to His saints.

label: Colossians 1:27
text: "Would make known" translates thelo, "desired" — underscoring that God's choice to reveal this mystery to the Gentiles was sheer grace, nothing they had earned. The "wealth" language is deliberate: unlike a national religion with boundaries, this mystery overflows every barrier of race or caste, and Paul calls that overflow itself the glory on display. "Christ in you" is present possession; "the hope of glory" is what's still ahead — believers already hold the reality in seed form, but its full unveiling waits for Christ's appearing.
translation: To whom God desired to make known what is the wealth of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of the glory.

label: Colossians 1:28
text: "Preach" here is katangello, "announce" — Paul isn't peddling a philosophy but broadcasting a fact. Alongside it stand two complementary verbs: noutheteo, "admonish," addressed to behavior needing correction, and didasko, "instruct," addressed to truth needing to be understood — warning paired with teaching the way repentance is paired with faith. "Every man" appears three times in one verse, a deliberate hammering against the Colossian teachers' claim to a higher wisdom reserved for the initiated few. And "perfect," teleios, borrows language from the pagan mystery cults for the fully initiated as opposed to the raw beginner — except Paul insists every believer, not a select group, is granted that full initiation in Christ.
translation: Whom we are continually announcing, admonishing every man and instructing every man in every kind of wisdom, so that we may present every man mature in Christ.

label: Colossians 1:29
text: "Labor" is kopiao, a term for the exhausting training of an athlete, and it primes the next verb, agonizomai, "to contend in the arena" — Paul pictures gospel ministry as strenuous, sweat-soaked effort, not passive waiting. The "working" that powers this labor is energeia (the root of our word "energy"), a term Paul reserves for superhuman power at work, whether God's or the devil's — here it's Christ's own energy operating in him, not human willpower stretched thin. Paul then extends the same athletic image, agon, "the arena of a contest," to describe his prayer life for churches he has never even visited in person — an inward wrestling match fought on their behalf. He wants their hearts "knit together" — a term for weaving or binding threads into a single fabric — resulting in the full assurance that comes from full knowledge, epignosis again, "of the mystery of God, Christ." The grammar puts "Christ" in apposition with "the mystery," meaning the two are the same thing: the mystery isn't information about Christ, it is Christ Himself, in whom every treasure of wisdom is kept — hidden not because it's withheld, but because, like buried treasure, it rewards only those willing to dig for it.
translation: To this end I am also continually laboring to the point of exhaustion, contending according to His energy, which is working powerfully in me. For I want you to know how great a struggle I am having on your behalf and on behalf of those in Laodicea and all who have not seen my face in the flesh, that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, resulting in all the wealth of full assurance of understanding, resulting in the full knowledge of the mystery of God, Christ — in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

label: Colossians 2:4
text: "Beguile" translates paralogizomai, literally "to reason alongside" — not an outright lie but a subtly skewed argument, reasoning that runs parallel to the truth just enough to mislead. "Enticing words" is pithanologia, built from "to persuade" and "word" — smooth, plausible-sounding argument, the kind that convinces by the sound of its logic rather than the substance of it.
translation: This I am saying so that no one may lead you astray by false reasoning, using persuasive, plausible-sounding speech.

label: Colossians 2:5
text: "Order" and "steadfastness" are both military terms — Paul, writing under armed guard in Rome, pictures the Colossians' faith as a well-drilled unit standing in formation, a solid front like a phalanx that can't be broken through. "Received," in the next section, is paralambano, "to take to one's side" — not merely hearing information but personally appropriating it, making the teaching about Christ one's own. Two participles then trace two different kinds of growth: "rooted" is perfect tense, describing a once-completed act, like a tree taking root, whose result now stands fixed and firm; "built up" is present tense, ongoing construction that never finishes. And it happens "in Him" rather than "upon Him" — Christ isn't merely the foundation the building rests on, He's the space the whole structure rises within.
translation: For even though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your orderly ranks and the solid front of your faith in Christ. So then, just as you took Christ Jesus the Lord to yourselves, keep ordering your behavior in Him — having been rooted, with the present result that you stand firm, and continually being built up in Him, and continually being made firm with reference to your faith, just as you were taught, overflowing with it in thanksgiving.

label: Colossians 2:8
text: "Beware" is a present imperative, "keep constantly on your guard" — an ongoing watchfulness, not a one-time alert. "Spoil" translates a verb used of carrying someone off as plunder or a captive slave — the false teaching doesn't just confuse, it enslaves. Paul's word for "philosophy" appears only this once in his letters; he isn't condemning the discipline broadly but "his philosophy" — a specific, article-marked system, "empty deceit" resting on paradosis, "handed-down tradition," the kind of chain-of-transmission authority the Colossian teachers claimed instead of any grounding in Scripture. He calls its content "elementary" — the same word for a child's basic lessons — beneath the maturity Christ actually offers.
translation: Keep constantly on guard, so that no one carries you off as plunder through his empty, deceptive philosophy — one resting on human tradition, on the elementary teachings of the world, and not on Christ.

label: Colossians 2:9
text: "Dwelleth" is present tense, katoikei, marking continuous, permanent residence, not a temporary visitation. "In bodily form" makes the point sharper still: the full weight of deity is at home in Christ specifically as one who possesses an actual human body, from His birth through His glorified, ascended state — not an abstraction hovering near Him but deity clothed in flesh. Greek actually has two different words behind our one English "deity" — one describes a general divine quality that reasoning from creation can dimly detect, the other describes full, personal Godhead. Paul reaches for the stronger of the two here: not that divine qualities radiate from Christ, but that absolute Godhead itself is what indwells Him.
translation: Because in Him, all the fulness of the Godhead continually and permanently makes its home, in bodily form.

label: Colossians 2:10
text: "Complete" is a perfect participle of the verb behind "fulness" itself — literally, "having been filled full, with the present result that you stand in a state of fulness." The logic runs: believers are first in Him, and being in Him, they are filled — not filled up in order to earn entry, but filled because they're already inside. Whatever the false teachers offered through their hierarchy of angelic mediators, Paul says believers already possess in Christ, who outranks every one of those powers as their Head.
translation: And you are in Him, having been completely filled full, with the present result that you stand in a state of fulness — in Him who is the Head of every ruler and authority.

label: Colossians 2:11
text: "Putting off" compounds two ideas of removal — stripping completely out of a garment and getting entirely away from it, more than simply taking off a coat; it's disposing of it for good. The best manuscripts read "the body of the flesh," not "the body of the sins of the flesh" — meaning the physical body itself, as it had been dominated by the sinful nature. That domination is what gets stripped away at conversion, not the sin nature's mere existence, which remains, but its controlling grip, broken and rendered powerless — the same point Paul makes in Romans when he says the body ruled by sin is "rendered inoperative." This, Paul says, is the real circumcision — not a cut in the flesh removing a small piece of the body, but a spiritual operation removing sin's whole controlling claim, done through Christ rather than by human hands.
translation: In whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not performed by human hands, in the stripping off and away from yourselves of the body of the flesh, by the circumcision that belongs to Christ.

label: Colossians 2:12
text: "Buried with Him" and "raised with Him" both build on the picture in Romans 6 — believers are placed into identification with Christ's death and resurrection through the Spirit's baptism, so that the power of sin is broken and a new, divine life is imparted. The "rising" in view here isn't the future bodily resurrection but a present, spiritual one — the same shift from spiritual death to spiritual life this letter has already described in chapter 1. That transfer happens through faith in the working of God — the same phrase used elsewhere for the display of power that raised Christ's actual body from the tomb, applied now to what happens inside a believing sinner.
translation: Having been buried with Him in that placing-into, in which placing-into you were also raised with Him, through your faith in the working of the God who raised Him out from among the dead.

label: Colossians 2:13
text: "Sins" is paraptoma, "a fall to the side" — a stumble off the intended path, in the dative case here, meaning the Colossians were dead "with reference to" their trespasses, not merely guilty of them. Their "uncircumcision" is named alongside their trespasses not for its literal, physical sense but as a symbol — the outward mark of an unchastened, ungoverned inner nature. "Quickened together" is one compound verb, "made alive together with" — the timing matters: this new life wasn't given piecemeal but all at once, in identification with the same historical moment Christ Himself was raised.
translation: And you, though dead with reference to your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, He made alive together with Him, having graciously forgiven us all our trespasses.

label: Colossians 2:14
text: "Blotting out" is a verb for erasing writing — wiping a wax tablet clean, not merely crossing it out but removing the record entirely. "Handwriting" is cheirographon, the technical term for a signed IOU, a bond of debt standing against the debtor until it's paid or cancelled. Paul pictures the law's claim on humanity as exactly this kind of legal debt-instrument, and says God didn't just discount it — He removed it "out of the midst," out of the place where a debtor's obligation would otherwise sit perpetually in view, embarrassing him at every turn — by nailing the actual document to the cross alongside Christ.
translation: Having wiped out the bond of debt consisting of decrees — the one that stood against us and was directly opposed to us — He has taken it completely out of the way, having nailed it to the cross.

label: Colossians 2:15
text:
"Stripped off" reuses the same verb from 2:11 for putting off the old self, now applied to the powers of darkness — Christ strips them the way a man strips off and discards a garment, then puts them on public display, a verb for publicly exhibiting something in shame, all pictured as a Roman triumphal procession, with the defeated powers marched behind the victor's chariot.

The next section names "eating," "drinking," "festival," "new moon," "Sabbath" — the Greek nouns are the acts themselves, the eating, the drinking, rather than food and drink as substances, pointing at ascetic self-denial rather than dietary law. Paul calls the whole system "a shadow of things to come" against "the body," meaning the substance — the reality the shadow only sketched has arrived in Christ, so going back to the shadow after the substance has appeared is backward.

"Beguile of reward" is a term from athletic judging — an umpire disqualifying a competitor and declaring him unworthy of the prize; the false teachers were setting themselves up as judges over other believers' spiritual standing. Their self-styled "humility" is undercut by the very next word, "delighting in" — a self-conscious, self-imposed performance rather than genuine lowliness, tangled up with a fixation on visions they claimed to have scrutinized minutely. Paul's sharpest jab is grammatical: the Greek word for "Head" is feminine, but the pronoun that follows it is masculine — breaking normal agreement on purpose, forcing the reader to hear "Head" as a person, not an abstraction, and that person is Christ, from whom the whole body — through its joints and ligaments — draws nourishment and grows with a growth that comes from God, not from angelic mediators.
translation: Having stripped off and away from Himself the rulers and authorities, He made a public display of them, leading them in triumphal procession. Therefore let no one judge you in the matter of eating or drinking, or with respect to a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath day — these are a shadow of what was coming, but the body, the substance, belongs to Christ. Let no one who delights in a self-imposed humility and the worship of angels disqualify you from your prize, going on at length about visions he has seen, being pointlessly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and not holding fast to the Head — from whom the whole body, being supplied and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that God supplies.

label: Colossians 2:20–23
text: "If ye be dead" isn't a hypothetical — the conditional particle plus indicative mood marks a fact already settled: "since, as is the case, you died with Christ." Having already died to these elemental teachings, Paul asks, why submit to them as though still alive under their rule? The prohibitions themselves stack up: "touch" pictures a deliberate, clinging contact, not an accidental brush, while "handle" describes only superficial contact — even a light, passing touch is forbidden by these rules. All of it, Paul notes dryly, concerns things "destined for corruption" in the very act of being used up — perishable stuff, hardly worth this much anxiety. The whole system is "self-devised worship" — a compound word meaning worship one invents and imposes on oneself rather than what God actually requires — paired with harsh, unsparing treatment of the body that has, Paul says bluntly, no actual value as a check on sensual indulgence. Ascetic severity and self-indulgence turn out to be the same problem wearing different clothes.
translation: Since, as is the case, you died with Christ, away from the elemental teachings of the world, why, as though still living in the world, do you let yourselves be subjected to decrees: Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle — all of which things are destined for decay in their very using — decrees according to the precepts and teachings of men? These things carry a reputation for wisdom in their self-devised worship, their affected humility, and their unsparing severity toward the body — but they hold no actual value against the indulgence of the flesh.

label: Colossians 3:2–4
text: "Set your affection" isn't just an emotional preference but phroneo, "direct your mind toward" — Paul already told them to seek things above; now he adds that they must think that way too, not merely act that way occasionally. "Ye are dead" is aorist, a completed past fact, not an ongoing process — the break from the old life happened, once, at conversion. Their new "life" is described as hidden — not absent, just currently concealed, the way a seed is fully alive underground before anything shows above the surface. And Paul doesn't merely say Christ gives that life; he says Christ is our life — identifying the believer's existence with Christ's own so closely that when He is revealed, so are they, sharing in the same glory.
translation: Keep your mind set on the things above, not on the things on the earth. For you died, and your life has been hidden with Christ in God. Whenever Christ, who is our life, is made visible, then you also will be made visible with Him in glory.

label: Colossians 3:5–7
text: "Mortify" is nekroo, "put to death" — an obsolete-sounding English word for a blunt Greek verb meaning to drain something of all power, to kill it outright rather than merely restrain it. The list that follows names the body's members not as body parts themselves but as instruments turned toward sin — sexual immorality in general, moral impurity, the filth of an indulgent life, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which Paul flatly calls idolatry — worship redirected from God to the desire for more. All of it describes how these believers "once walked" — their entire manner of life used to be bounded by this list, with nothing in it that pleased God.
translation: Put to death, once for all, your members that belong to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, depraved passion, evil desire, and the greed that amounts to idolatry — because of these things the wrath of God is coming. In these very things you also once walked, when you were living in them.

label: Colossians 3:8
text: "Anger" and "wrath" name two different tempers, not the same sin twice: the first is the slow-burning, settled grudge that nurses a plan of revenge, while the second is the sudden boil-over, a flash flood of temper. "Malice" adds active ill-will, the desire to actually harm someone; "blasphemy" here means slander against another person's reputation, not only against God; "filthy communication" is specifically obscene, foul-mouthed speech. Four words, four distinct ways anger leaks out — cold, hot, malicious, and coarse.
translation: But now put away, all of it, once for all: settled, vengeful anger, sudden bursts of wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk out of your mouth.

label: Colossians 3:9–11
text:
"Stop lying" uses a present imperative with a negative — grammar for halting an action already in progress, not warning against a future one; these believers were still lying to each other and needed to quit. The "old man" gets "stripped off" with the same forceful verb used earlier for stripping off the body dominated by sin — a decisive, once-for-all removal, not a gradual fade. The "new man" is "constantly being renewed" — present tense, ongoing — after the image of the Creator, echoing Genesis without claiming to be a second Genesis: as the first man bore God's image at creation, the new man bears it again in re-creation. And where that renewal has taken hold, Paul says there simply "cannot be" distinctions of race, culture, or class — not merely that such distinctions don't matter but that they have become impossible categories in Christ: Greek, Jew, barbarian, slave, free — categories that once divided the whole ancient world into privileged and unprivileged, all rendered void.

"Put on" then shifts to a command in the aorist — do it at once, not gradually — clothing yourselves in the temperament fitting for God's "chosen ones," a word implying selection out of the crowd. The list of virtues that follows draws on a Hebrew sense of the "inward parts" as the seat of tender affection rather than violent passion — compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, the willingness to accept even hard treatment without fighting back, and patience toward difficult people. "Forgiving" shares its root with the word for grace itself — to forgive is to extend the same kind of favor God has already extended, in the same measure He extended it.
translation: Stop lying to one another, since you have stripped off the old self with its practices, and have clothed yourselves with the new self, which is continually being renewed to a full knowledge, according to the image of the One who created it — a state in which there cannot be Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all things and in all. Put on, then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved: a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, bearing with one another and freely forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another — just as, and to the extent that, the Lord forgave you, so also you must forgive.

label: Colossians 3:14
text: "Above all these" pictures love as the outer garment thrown over everything already put on — not one virtue among many but the sash that holds the rest in place. "Bond" is a word for a binding cord or ligament, and "perfectness" describes not sinless flawlessness but completeness — the result you get only when every virtue is bound together into one working whole rather than scattered pieces. Without love, Paul implies, the other virtues stay loose and disconnected, however good each looks on its own.
translation: And upon all these, put on love, which is the binding cord of completeness.

label: Colossians 3:15
text:
"Rule" translates a term from athletic contests for an umpire's decision — Paul pictures "the peace of Christ" stepping into the tug-of-war among competing impulses in the heart and calling the decisive verdict, the way an umpire settles a disputed play. That peace isn't only personal; it's the peace "into which you were called in one body" — corporate, binding the whole church together, not just each believer's private calm.

The "word of Christ" is to "dwell" richly — the same word used earlier for deity being "at home" in Christ, now applied to Scripture taking up permanent residence in the believer, richly, not sparsely. Paul distinguishes three overlapping categories of song — one leaning toward the Psalms of David, one toward newly composed Christian praise, and a general umbrella term covering any spiritual song — while singing "with grace," the definite article marking out a specific, Spirit-supplied grace rather than singing talent, since the Greek word for grace doubles as the word for thanksgiving.
translation: And let the peace of Christ act as umpire in your hearts — the peace to which you were also called in one body. And be continually thankful. Let the word of Christ make its home in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, continually giving thanks to God the Father through Him.

label: Colossians 3:18–22
text: "Fitting" appears in the imperfect tense — "was fitting," pointing back to the very moment these believers entered the Christian life, as if the obligation were self-evident from the start rather than newly imposed. For husbands, the command is to love with the word for God's own self-giving love, not the ordinary affection that brought them to the altar in the first place — this is love as self-denial, the kind shown at the cross, deliberately distinguished from mere fondness. "Provoke" toward children is a word for irritation that, left unchecked, breeds a settled discouragement — Paul traces cause and effect: needless exasperation produces disheartened kids. "Eyeservice" is one compound word for work done only under a watching eye — service calibrated to whether the boss is looking — set against "singleness of heart," undivided effort whether observed or not.
translation: Wives, keep yourselves in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives with a self-giving love, and do not be embittered against them. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is well-pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they do not lose heart. Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with an undivided heart, fearing the Lord.

label: Colossians 3:23–25
text: "Whatever you do" uses two different Greek verbs for "do" in the same sentence — the first a generic word for performing an action, the second specifically "labor, work hard," opposed to idleness. Paul isn't asking for mere compliance but diligence, done "from the soul," heart-deep rather than surface-level. "Reward" is a requital paid back in kind, and the phrase "of the inheritance" functions as an equation — the reward is the inheritance, not a bonus alongside it. Masters get their own coda in the next verse: what they owe their slaves is "equity" — not literal sameness of social condition but the fair, even-handed treatment due a fellow believer, since the master too answers to a Master in heaven.
translation: Whatever you do, work at it heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive back the inheritance as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no favoritism. Masters, grant your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

label: Colossians 4:2–4
text: "Continue" is proskartereo, unremitting, persistent attention — not occasional prayer but a habit sustained without letting up. Paired with it, "watch" warns against the specific danger of long, sustained prayer going slack — staying spiritually alert even while praying at length, since drowsy prayer easily becomes empty repetition. Paul's request for himself is for "a door of the word" — a specific opening to preach, not vague success — appropriate for a man who describes his imprisonment with a perfect-tense verb: "I have been bound, with the present result that I remain in a bound state," a chain that was, at the moment of writing, still literally attached to his wrist.
translation: Devote yourselves to prayer with unremitting attention, staying alert in it with thanksgiving, praying at the same time also for us, that God would open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, on account of which I have been bound and remain bound, that I may make it clear, as it is necessary for me to speak.

label: Colossians 4:5
text: "Redeeming the time" pictures buying up an opportunity before it's gone — a marketplace verb, "to purchase for oneself," and "time" here is kairos, not the ordinary word for duration but a strategic, ripe moment. Paul's exhortation is toward "those without," outsiders to the faith — wise conduct toward them is itself a kind of shrewd buying, seizing brief windows to do good before they close.
translation: Order your behavior wisely toward those outside, buying up for yourselves every strategic opportunity.

label: Colossians 4:6
text: "Seasoned with salt" carries a double sense in the ancient world — salt both flavors food, making it palatable and pleasant, and preserves it from spoiling. Paul's picture of speech "seasoned with salt" is speech that is both agreeable to hear and free of corruption — pleasant without being rotten underneath. The goal is knowing how to answer "each one" individually — not a stock response but conversation tailored to the person in front of you.
translation: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned throughout with salt, so that you may know how it is necessary for you to answer each person.

label: Colossians 4:7–9
text: "Fellow-servant," literally "fellow-bondslave," is Paul's way of placing Tychicus on the same level as himself before Christ — no hierarchy, both owned by the same Master. "I have sent" is what grammarians call the epistolary aorist: Paul writes from the vantage point of his readers, describing the sending as already complete because by the time they read the letter, it will be. Onesimus travels with Tychicus carrying his own quiet transformation in the sentence structure — once known to the Colossians only as a runaway slave, he's introduced here simply as "the faithful and beloved brother, one of you," his old status left entirely unmentioned.
translation: Tychicus will make known to you all my circumstances — the beloved brother, faithful servant, and fellow-bondslave in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts — together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is happening here.

label: Colossians 4:14
text: "Physician" is this brief mention's sole biblical note identifying Luke's profession — a detail that colors how carefully he researched and wrote his Gospel and Acts, with the trained observational habits of a doctor. Paul's warmth shows in the added word "beloved," while in the very same breath Demas gets nothing but his bare name — no epithet, no praise, a silence that reads as ominous next to Luke's warm commendation, especially in light of what later happens to Demas.
translation: Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.

label: Colossians 4:15
text: "The church in her house" — the Greek pronoun in the best manuscripts is feminine, identifying Nympha as a woman leading a congregation that met under her own roof, at a time before any dedicated church buildings existed anywhere in the Roman world; the earliest churches were, without exception, someone's living room.
translation: Greet the brothers in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the church in her house.

label: Colossians 4:16
text: "The letter from Laodicea" is one of the New Testament's small mysteries — a letter of Paul's, now lost, or possibly an early title for what we know as Ephesians, meant to circulate as a general letter among several churches rather than address only one. Whichever it was, Paul's instruction pictures early congregations trading correspondence, treating apostolic letters as shared property meant for wider circulation, not private mail to one church alone.
translation: And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is read also in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.

label: Colossians 4:17
text: "Fulfil" is a verb meaning "discharge completely" — not merely perform a duty but carry it through to its full extent. The added emphasis Paul places on this one-line message to Archippus suggests a ministry of some real weight, not routine service, and a man who may have needed the nudge to see it all the way through.
translation: And say to Archippus: Look to the ministry you received in the Lord, that you fulfill it completely.

label: Colossians 4:18
text: "With my own hand" marks a shift — everything before this line was dictated to a secretary; Paul takes the pen himself only for the closing greeting, a habit that also guarded against forged letters circulating under his name. "Remember my bonds" lands with quiet weight: as he wrote it, an actual chain was fastened to his wrist, and the simple request asks for exactly what a chained man most needs — not to be forgotten by the people he can no longer visit.
translation: The greeting is in my own hand — Paul's. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
